text:
marco: quick follow-up to the continuous-batcher RFC: customers and internal tests show a short but painful enqueue-to-serve tail for tenants that were evicted ~1-2s before a burst. need to decide an approach for reducing the rehydrate penalty. link: https://rfc.internal/continuous-batcher#rehydration

ellen: can you show the simplest repro? even synthetic load would help.

marco: repro sketch - low-rate tenant sends one req/min for a while. soft-lease TTL=60s. after TTL they lose headroom. when they suddenly send a 10qps burst, we see a median extra delay ~180ms and 99p ~420ms while allocator reassigns tokens. trace:
```ntrace=tx-ef12
0ms enqueue
60010ms lease_expire
60150ms enqueue_burst
60220ms allocate_start
60290ms allocate_done
60310ms serve_start
```

sam: that 70-150ms allocate window is the regress. Two broad fixes: 1) keep tiny per-tenant tail reserve after expiry, or 2) loan short-lived credits from a transient-credit-pool on first enqueue post-eviction.

priya: tail reserve keeps accounting simple but reduces packing efficiency. transient pool seems attractive if we strictly cap it.

ellen: how would transient pool work? sketch pls.

sam: idea: allocator exposes borrow_transient(tenant, tokens, ttl_ms). It hands out tokens from a global transient bucket (configurable percent of pool). Borrowed tokens come with auto-release after ttl_ms. Borrow only on first enqueue after a lease is absent, limited to X concurrent loans/tenant.

marco: advantages: minimal lease-state changes, fast to A/B. cons: adds short-term accounting surface and needs telemetry to ensure it isn't increasing cost.

priya: failure modes: noisy tenant could repeatedly borrow and release causing oscillation. Mitigations: per-tenant loan cooldown, loan-count limit, reward-based gating linking loan eligibility to recent average qps.

ellen: alternative: grace state on expiry where a tenant keeps a micro-credit (e.g., 5 tokens) for G ms with preemption allowed. If no activity, credits reclaimed. That keeps viewable invariants in lease manager.

sam: tradeoff summary: transient-pool = low-touch in allocator, easier rollback; grace-state = cleaner model but touches lease reconciliation + autoscaler triggers.

marco: metrics to add for experiment: enqueue_to_serve_ms histogram (labels: tenant, cohort), transient_loan_grants_total, loan_fail_retries, lease_eviction_count, pool_utilization_pct. example query: avg_over_time(histogram_quantile(0.95, enqueue_to_serve_ms_bucket{service="continuous-batcher"})[1h])

priya: experiment plan: enable transient-pool for 5% of staging pool; A/B across 50 internal tenants for 12h; success if 95p enqueue_to_serve drops by >20% and pool token-cost delta <1.2%. Safety: global transient cap, per-tenant cap=30 tokens, cooldown=1s then *2 backoff.

sam: implementation note: allocator has allocate_for_tenant(tenant, tokens, mode). I'll add mode=transient which maps to borrow_transient under the hood. Keep the API idempotent.

ellen: ownership: I'll do metrics PR. Marco, can you open allocator PR and test harness? Priya, write safety guardrails. CI-bot will queue a canary deploy after PRs land.

ci-bot: canary deploy scheduled: batcher/transient-loans -> canary-1 at 2024-05-03T09:00:00Z :rocket:

marco: thanks. I'll post a follow-up with the experiment dashboard link once wired. If anyone thinks we should do grace-state first instead, speak now. :eyes:
